Below is a comprehensive, theory-grounded review of “barriers,” “challenges,” and “obstacles,” their conceptual differences, and the theoretical foundations you can deploy for a master’s thesis. The review synthesizes cross-domain definitions, major models and frameworks, and practical ways to map and analyze barriers to use, with attention to how to build theoretical sensitivity and an actionable conceptual map.

Conceptual foundations: what are barriers, challenges, and obstacles?
Across domains, barriers, challenges, and obstacles are closely related yet carry distinct emphases. A baseline definition treats a barrier as anything that impedes progress toward a goal, with challenges and obstacles often used interchangeably to denote impediments that require removal, adaptation, or creative problem-solving to overcome <cite id="565a2ab8-0">Barriers are obstacles or challenges that hinder the progress or achievement of goals</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-1">Barriers are often impediments and obstacles that obstruct progress and the achievement of goals, and overcoming them requires creative management and mindset change</cite>. Conceptual metaphor work shows how “business is a journey,” where barriers are structured impediments such as entry barriers, switching barriers, and barriers to imitation—illustrating how domain-specific “barriers” become strategic constructs <cite id="565a2ab8-2">In business, barriers like entry barriers, barriers to imitation, and exit barriers illustrate numerous obstacles in business activities</cite>. Education provides a clear typology: internal (cognitive, emotional) versus external (ecological, institutional) learning barriers, together with teacher-facing challenges in addressing them, highlighting the duality of personal and contextual constraints <cite id="565a2ab8-3">Learning barriers impede knowledge/skill acquisition and can be internal (cognitive/emotional) or external (ecological/resources), with teachers facing challenges in identification, resource limitations, and classroom management</cite>. Cyberbullying research operationalizes barriers into six categories (psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, prevention/intervention) and visualizes them as a conceptual map—useful for structuring a comprehensive obstacle taxonomy and mitigation plan <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Barriers and challenges were categorized into psychological, social/cultural, awareness and reporting, legal and policy, technological, and prevention/intervention, and illustrated in a conceptual map</cite>.

Theoretical families organizing “barriers” to use and change

1) Individual behavior and technology acceptance (TAM/UTAUT/IRT)
Technology acceptance models treat barriers as determinant factors shaping intention and use. TAM posits perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as primary drivers; ease of use positively influences usefulness, and both shape adoption behavior <cite id="f40d5515-0">Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are the main determinants of technology acceptance, with ease of use positively influencing usefulness</cite>. UTAUT integrates determinants across eight prior theories into performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, and has demonstrated stronger explanatory power for usage intention and behavior than earlier models (often up to ~70% variance explained), making it a robust lens to identify barriers at individual and organizational levels <cite id="f40d5515-1">UTAUT integrates determinants from TRA, TAM, TPB, MM, MPCU, IDT, and SCT into performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions</cite><cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT identifies performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, and has shown higher explanatory power than prior models (up to ~70% of variance in intention and 50% in use)</cite><cite id="f40d5515-4">Compared with earlier models (17%–42% variance), UTAUT achieves up to 70% explanatory power, making it effective for analyzing technology acceptance</cite>. Innovation resistance theory (IRT) explicitly categorizes barriers into functional (risk, value, usage) and psychological (traditional, image) types, especially salient in early adoption stages and often integrated with UTAUT/TAM to diagnose adoption barriers <cite id="f40d5515-0">Innovation resistance theory categorizes innovation resistance into functional barriers (risk, value, usage) and psychological barriers (traditional, image), and is frequently integrated with UTAUT or TAM</cite>. These models offer measurable constructs (e.g., effort expectancy as a barrier, facilitating conditions as enablers), enabling empirical testing and intervention design in a master’s thesis.

2) Organizational change and resistance (Kotter, Lewin; multidimensional resistance)
Organizational transformation repeatedly encounters resistance as a key obstacle; change models emphasize that resistance must be managed, not merely eliminated, with strategies such as creating urgency, strong leadership, phased communication, and adaptive, iterative management <cite id="317e1c0d-0">Resistance to change is a common obstacle in organizational transformation and must be managed</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Resistance emerges from individual fears (job loss, skill gaps) and structural issues (leadership, cultural misfit), with barriers including poor communication, low perceived value, and limited training; strategies include leadership commitment, phased communication, and adaptive piloting with feedback loops</cite>. Contemporary frameworks show resistance is multidimensional—cognitive, affective, and intentional—and may be outspoken or silent, deliberate or non-deliberate, directed at the process, change itself, or the technology; they also attend to who resists and over time, making resistance a signal guiding more resilient practices <cite id="317e1c0d-2">Resistance is multidimensional (cognitive, affective, intentional) and may be outspoken/silent, deliberate/non-deliberate, with temporal and stakeholder specificity; frameworks help understand and manage resistance as a signal for resilient practices</cite>. Adaptive-cycle and holistic approaches map where resistance concentrates across stages and how management styles and stakeholder needs interact with technological change, reinforcing that barriers are dynamic and context-contingent <cite id="317e1c0d-4">A holistic approach integrates the Adaptive Cycle of Resilience, Maslow’s theory, and organizational models to identify where resistance concentrates across stages and how management styles and stakeholder needs shape technological change</cite><cite id="f40d5515-1">Change models such as Lewin and Kotter underpin strategies to address resistance in technology adoption</cite>. Conceptually, TAM/UTAUT capture proximal, individual-level barriers, while organizational change theories capture distal, structural, cultural, and power-related barriers; together they cover the full barrier stack for “use.”

3) Socio-technical, institutional, and contingency perspectives (organizational theory, legitimacy, networks)
Implementation science shows barriers and facilitators span levels: intervention characteristics, inner/outer settings, individuals, and process. CFIR synthesizes 29 theories into five domains and 39 constructs, offering uniform language to compare barriers and facilitators across contexts and interventions, including networks/legitimacy and readiness—directly linking organizational theory to implementation barriers <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR constructs synthesize 29 organizational and implementation theories to identify, organize, and communicate barriers and facilitators across organizations</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Organizational theory specifies cross-level influences (environment to behavior), supports constructs like interagency networks (cosmopolitanism) for resource access, highlights legitimacy and contingency pressures, and cautions that superficial implementation can occur to gain legitimacy</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR’s five domains—intervention characteristics, inner setting, outer setting, individual characteristics, and process—provide a common structure for implementation barriers and facilitators across diverse initiatives</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-3">CFIR specifies 39 constructs across five domains influencing implementation, integrating determinant theories</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR provides a determinant framework with 26 constructs across five domains, is suited for studying barriers and facilitators, and is widely used for cross-setting comparisons</cite>. These frameworks align with socio-technical thinking: technical constraints (e.g., complexity, cost) interact with social-ecological constraints (e.g., culture, networks, legitimacy), and contingency theories argue that successful “use” requires adaptation to context; resistance may persist when interventions are not adapted to local norms and resources <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Contingency theories suggest successful implementation requires adaptation to unique organizational context, while threats to autonomy or resources undermine sustainment; institutional pressures can drive superficial implementation for legitimacy</cite>. Conceptually, this positions barriers as emergent intersections of technical and socio-institutional layers, where “barriers to use” include misfit with existing practices, legitimacy deficits, and network-access constraints.

4) Complexity, chaos, and dynamic systems (adaptive cycles; iterative feedback)
Adaptive-cycle models (e.g., Panarchy/ACoR) depict organizations as complex systems where resistance and change interlock across stages (e.g., exploitation, conservation, release, reorganization), implying that barriers shift with system state and require staged, iterative responses. Integrating such models with motivation and management theories clarifies when resistance is most likely and how leadership and information systems can recalibrate pathways <cite id="317e1c0d-4">Resistance peaks at identifiable stages in the Adaptive Cycle; management styles and stakeholder needs shape outcomes, and information systems influence change trajectories</cite>. In fast-moving digital transformation, linear models are challenged by nonlinearity and speed; strategies pivot to piloting and feedback loops that treat resistance as diagnostic data to redesign processes and roles <cite id="317e1c0d-1">The rapid pace of technological change requires adaptive, iterative management with piloting and feedback loops; resistance reflects individual and structural issues and signals where practices must become more resilient</cite>. This emphasizes barriers as dynamic constraints within complex systems, not static impediments, motivating mixed-methods designs that capture feedback and evolution.

5) Design/UX and customer discovery (obstacles to use as user-experience constraints)
User-centered perspectives treat “barriers to use” as anti-affordances and pain points in interaction—frictions that hinder goals and must be removed or reframed through empathic design. Cyberbullying SLR exemplifies structured categorization of barriers across psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, and prevention/intervention domains; you can adapt this into “obstacle taxonomies” for your context, mapping each obstacle to user stories, personas, and journey stages and visualizing them in a system map <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Barriers and challenges were categorized into psychological, social/cultural, awareness and reporting, legal and policy, technological, and prevention/intervention, and illustrated in a conceptual map</cite>. Conceptually, barriers here are visible UX constraints plus latent, context-dependent constraints (e.g., policy or cultural norms), and challenges become hypotheses about redesigns to restore affordance–constraint balance.

6) Implementation science barriers–facilitators frameworks (CFIR-informed)
For interventions and programs, CFIR offers the most widely used determinant framework to systematically elicit barriers and facilitators across five domains and 39 constructs, enabling cross-setting comparisons and consistent coding. It is not a single theory but a meta-framework that integrates organizational, sociocultural, and process determinants, and is increasingly used to compare barriers across multiple, distinct initiatives within one organization—a powerful approach for mapping organizational obstacles to adoption, implementation, and sustainment <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR provides a standard, evidence-based path to identify, organize, and communicate barriers and facilitators</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR’s five domains structure the analysis of common implementation barriers and facilitators across diverse initiatives</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR’s scope, clarity, and widespread use enable comparison of barriers and facilitators within and across contexts</cite>. In practice, CFIR supports grounded coding of qualitative data (e.g., interviews, observations) and quantitative indicators (e.g., relative advantage, complexity, cost) into barrier/facilitator categories, which is ideal for a master’s thesis that integrates mixed methods.

Distinguishing barriers, challenges, and obstacles: conceptual map and relationships
- Barriers: structural or contextual impediments that limit the possibility of intended actions; can be positive (protective) or negative (impediments), and may be designed or emergent; negative barriers obstruct progress and require removal or work-around <cite id="565a2ab8-1">Barriers can be positively designed as protective mechanisms or negatively function as impediments/obstacles that obstruct progress and must be removed; overcoming them often requires creative thinking and mindset change</cite>.
- Challenges: framed as tasks or problems to be solved; often bridge the gap between goal and barrier, involving skills, resources, and strategies to negotiate constraints; in metaphor, challenges resemble terrain irregularities and domain-specific constraints (entry/exit/imitation barriers) <cite id="565a2ab8-2">Organizational “journey” metaphors map challenges to entry/exit/imitation barriers that complicate strategy and movement</cite>.
- Obstacles: concrete manifestations of barriers—tangible frictions, risks, or constraints that block use or delay outcomes; often categorized by domain (psychological, social, organizational, technological, policy, process) and by level (individual, team, organizational, ecosystem) <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Barriers were categorized into psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, and prevention/intervention domains</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-3">Barriers span internal (cognitive/emotional) and external (ecological, resource) levels</cite>.

Mapping theoretical lenses to levels and types of barriers
- Individual/behavioral: TAM/UTAUT/IRT identify proximal determinants and resistance roots; measure barriers as low performance expectancy, high effort expectancy, poor facilitating conditions, functional/psychological resistance; interventions include training, communication, reframing usefulness/ease <cite id="f40d5515-0">TAM/UTAUT/IRT provide determinants (usefulness, ease, facilitating conditions, resistance types) and integrative frameworks for adoption barriers</cite><cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT’s determinants and moderators enable diagnosing and addressing adoption barriers</cite>.
- Organizational/cultural: change models and organizational theory add power, legitimacy, network, and contingency pressures; barriers include resistance, lack of alignment, legitimacy deficits, resource constraints; strategies include leadership, staged communication, legitimacy-building audits, and adaptive redesign <cite id="317e1c0d-1">Resistance reflects individual fears and structural issues; strategies include leadership commitment and adaptive piloting</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Organizational theories highlight interagency networks, legitimacy pressures, and contingency adaptation as determinants and barriers</cite>.
- Socio-technical/complexity: CFIR and adaptive cycle models show barriers emerge at intervention, inner/outer settings, individuals, and process levels; barriers are interdependent and evolve; mapping with CFIR and iterative feedback loops helps reveal feedback loops and cross-level influences <cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR’s five domains and 26 constructs provide a comprehensive list of barriers and facilitators across levels</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-4">Resistance concentrates at specific adaptive cycle stages and interacts with leadership and stakeholder needs</cite>.
- Design/UX: user-centered and customer discovery lenses frame obstacles as anti-affordances and journey frictions; structured taxonomies like psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, and prevention/intervention guide obstacle elicitation and systematization <cite id="565a2ab8-4">A six-category obstacle taxonomy with conceptual mapping supports diagnosis and mitigation</cite>.

Operationalization: coding, measurement, and methods
- Elicitation and categorization: Use CFIR-informed constructs to code barriers/facilitators; for digital tools, adapt TAM/UTAUT determinants into survey items (e.g., effort expectancy as perceived difficulty; facilitating conditions as organizational support) and combine with qualitative probes to capture latent barriers (norms, legitimacy) <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR provides standard terminology to identify and organize barriers and facilitators</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR specifies constructs across five domains for coding and analysis</cite><cite id="f40d5515-0">Perceived ease of use and usefulness can be measured as barriers to adoption; facilitating conditions capture organizational enablers</cite>.
- Mixed-methods triangulation: Pair quantitative determinants (UTAUT scales) with qualitative data (semi-structured interviews, diaries, journey mapping) to surface silent or non-observable resistance and contextual constraints; apply adaptive-cycle checkpoints to sequence interventions in pilots and feedback loops <cite id="317e1c0d-1">Adaptive management with piloting and feedback loops addresses resistance and process frictions</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-2">Frameworks capture outspoken and silent, observable and non-observable resistance, and specify what is being resisted and by whom</cite>.
- Visual analytics: Build conceptual maps and obstacle matrices similar to the cyberbullying SLR—axes such as “visibility vs. latency” (awareness/reporting vs. internal cognitive barriers), “controllability” (individual skills vs. policy/legal constraints), and “time horizon” (immediate UX frictions vs. structural/long-term network/legitimacy barriers) <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Conceptual maps illustrate categories of barriers and challenges to guide responses</cite>.
- Action planning: For each obstacle category, specify mitigation levers aligned to theory level—individual (training, change management), organizational (leadership, resource allocation, adaptation), and ecosystem (policy alignment, legitimacy strategies) <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Legitimacy, networks, and contingency adaptation suggest concrete levers (e.g., stakeholder engagement, resource access, legitimacy audits)</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Leadership commitment, phased communication, and adaptive piloting are effective strategies for overcoming resistance</cite>.

A conceptual map for your master’s thesis: integrating theories and levels
1) Define scope and perspective
- Choose whether you study “use” of a digital tool, adoption/implementation of a program, organizational transformation, user experience of a service, or cross-level integration; each scope aligns differently with theories <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR aligns to organizational implementation across multiple interventions</cite><cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT aligns to individual/organizational adoption of technologies</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Resistance frameworks align to organizational change under digital transformation</cite>.
- Articulate initial equivalence: barriers as obstacles/challenges to “use,” mapped by domain and level (individual, team, organization, ecosystem), and differentiated by visibility, controllability, and time horizon <cite id="565a2ab8-0">Barriers are obstacles/challenges that hinder goal progress</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-3">Internal and external barriers define personal vs. contextual constraints</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-4">Domain categories structure observable challenge types</cite>.

2) Theoretical backbone: stack models to cover proximal–distal and technical–social–institutional layers
- Proximal behavior: TAM/UTAUT/IRT to capture perceived usefulness/ease, facilitating conditions, and resistance types; hypothesize that higher effort expectancy and lower facilitating conditions predict lower use <cite id="f40d5515-0">Perceived usefulness and ease of use drive intention; facilitating conditions and resistance types shape adoption</cite><cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT’s determinants and moderators provide a robust explanatory base for adoption barriers</cite>.
- Organizational/cultural: Kotter/Lewin/change management for resistance management; organizational theory for networks, legitimacy, and contingency—hypothesize that legitimacy deficits, weak networks, and misfit with context impede sustainment <cite id="317e1c0d-0">Resistance to change is a common obstacle and must be managed</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Networks, legitimacy, and contingency adaptation are critical determinants and barriers</cite>.
- Socio-technical/complexity: CFIR domains to structure cross-level barriers; adaptive cycle to sequence interventions; hypothesize that misalignment across intervention characteristics, inner/outer settings, and process domains produces emergent obstacles and requires iterative feedback <cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR’s five domains structure barriers and facilitators across initiatives</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-4">Adaptive-cycle stages map where resistance concentrates; iterative strategies adjust management and stakeholder engagement</cite>.
- UX/design: user-centered taxonomies to identify anti-affordances; hypothesize that reducing friction in awareness, access, and interaction directly increases use <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, and prevention/intervention categories capture actionable UX and policy obstacles</cite>.

3) Data strategies aligned to theory and level
- Quantitative: UTAUT-based survey with effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions; analyze associations with self-reported use and performance; include moderators (age/experience/voluntariness) <cite id="f40d5515-1">UTAUT determinants and moderators guide survey design and analysis</cite><cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT explains substantial variance in intention and use, supporting predictive modeling</cite>.
- Qualitative: semi-structured interviews and observations to surface silent resistance, cultural norms, and legitimacy concerns; memoing around CFIR constructs to code barriers/facilitators; journey mapping to sequence obstacles over time and touchpoints <cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR constructs across five domains provide a coding scheme for barriers and facilitators</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-2">Frameworks differentiate outspoken vs. silent, observable vs. non-observable resistance and specify targets</cite>.
- Experiments/pilots: A/B tests of UX redesigns; small-scale pilots with feedback loops to test process adaptations and measure impact on adoption and efficiency <cite id="317e1c0d-1">Phased communication, leadership commitment, and adaptive piloting with feedback loops are effective strategies</cite>.

4) Synthesis and intervention logic
- Build a barrier–leverage matrix mapping each obstacle to theory-informed levers (e.g., UX redesign for effort expectancy; training and coaching; leadership sponsorship; policy/legal alignment; network building) and to process steps (planning, engaging, executing, reflecting, evaluating) in CFIR <cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR specifies process steps (planning, engaging, executing, reflecting, evaluating) to structure mitigation</cite><cite id="f40d5515-0">Reducing effort and enhancing facilitating conditions directly target adoption barriers</cite>.
- Use conceptually grounded “obstacle-to-insight” narratives: for each barrier category, narrate how it constrains use, why (mechanism from theory), and how to transform constraints into facilitators through co-design, policy change, or structural adaptation <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Organizational theory suggests adapting interventions to context, engaging networks for resources, and auditing legitimacy to convert barriers into facilitators</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-1">Overcoming obstacles often requires creative management and mindset change, turning impediments into enablers</cite>.

Sensitizing concepts and theoretical sensitivity
- Barriers are multilevel and dynamic: Do not treat resistance as merely “people problems.” Separate structural/cultural constraints (outer setting, process) from proximal UX and individual perceptions (inner setting, characteristics), and sequence interventions across adaptive-cycle stages <cite id="8b19d7a4-2">Intervention characteristics, outer setting, and process domains distinguish structural from proximal barriers</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-4">Resistance likelihood varies across adaptive-cycle stages, requiring staged strategies</cite>.
- Barriers often encode legitimacy and power: Institutional pressures can drive superficial adoption; legitimacy deficits and network disconnection are hidden barriers that manifest as “non-adherence” even when barriers are removed at the UX level. Audit legitimacy cues and stakeholder power dynamics <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Superficial implementation for legitimacy can undermine objectives; legitimacy and networks are key determinants that must be addressed to convert barriers into facilitators</cite>.
- Barriers are context-contingent: Contingency theories warn that “one-size-fits-all” solutions fail; treat your intervention as contingent—adaptability, relative advantage, and trialability are determinants; design for fit, not just function <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Successful implementation likely requires adaptation to unique organizational context; threats to autonomy or resources impede sustainment</cite><cite id="f40d5515-0">Perceived usefulness and ease of use are subjective and context-dependent determinants</cite>.
- Obstacles can be productive signals: Resistance and reporting barriers may reveal risks and misalignments; treat them as diagnostic data to refine design and strategy, not merely as impediments to remove <cite id="317e1c0d-2">Resistance can highlight potential flaws or risks and requires understanding root concerns across cognitive, affective, and intentional dimensions</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Resistance signals structural issues (leadership, culture) and individual fears, guiding resilient practices</cite>.

Putting it all together: a step-by-step blueprint for your thesis
1) Scope and problem framing: Define “use” precisely (frequency, appropriateness, outcomes), identify the population/setting, and select your focal theory stack (e.g., TAM/UTAUT for adoption + CFIR for organizational implementation + change models for resistance) <cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT’s multi-level framing suits organizational adoption studies</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR structures barriers and facilitators across organizational domains</cite>.
2) Conceptual map: Draw a multi-level barrier map combining individual determinants (usefulness/ease/facilitating conditions, resistance types), organizational/cultural (power, legitimacy, networks), and socio-technical/complexity (inner/outer settings, process) with UX categories (psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, prevention/intervention) <cite id="f40d5515-0">TAM/UTAUT provide proximal constructs</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR’s five domains and 26 constructs supply comprehensive coding</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-4">Obstacle categories guide structured categorization and visualization</cite>.
3) Measurement plan: Build a mixed-methods design—UTAUT-based survey plus interviews/observations coded with CFIR constructs; include pilot experiments to test UX/process interventions; sequence checkpoints aligned to adaptive-cycle stages <cite id="f40d5515-1">UTAUT integrates determinants for survey modeling</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR constructs enable qualitative coding across domains</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Adaptive piloting with feedback loops operationalizes iterative strategies</cite>.
4) Analysis and synthesis: Quantitatively test determinants with regression/path models; qualitatively identify barrier narratives and their cross-level linkages; build a barrier–leverage matrix mapping obstacles to theory-informed levers and CFIR process steps; visualize as an obstacle-to-insight pathway <cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT’s explanatory power supports predictive modeling of adoption barriers</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR standardizes terminology to generalize findings across settings</cite>.
5) Implications: Design interventions that convert latent barriers into facilitators—trainability and support for effort expectancy, co-design to enhance usefulness, leadership sponsorship for legitimacy, network and policy alignment for outer-setting constraints, and iterative feedback loops to sustain change <cite id="f40d5515-0">Facilitating conditions and ease of use are levers to reduce adoption barriers</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Legitimacy-building, network engagement, and adaptation to context convert barriers into facilitators</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Leadership and communication strategies address structural and individual resistance</cite>.

Illustrative examples to inspire your literature synthesis
- Education: Learning barriers span internal (motivation, anxiety) and external (resources, access), with teachers facing challenges in classroom management and coordination—implying that “barriers to use” include both student-level perceptions and school-level supports <cite id="565a2ab8-3">Internal and external learning barriers impede acquisition; teachers face resource and support challenges in addressing them</cite>.
- Digital transformation: Resistance to new systems arises from fears and structural misfit; effective strategies include leadership commitment, phased communication, and piloted feedback loops—connecting TAM/UTAUT determinants to organizational change tactics <cite id="317e1c0d-1">Resistance stems from individual and structural issues; leadership and adaptive piloting mitigate barriers</cite>.
- Health programs: CFIR-based scoping reviews map barriers/facilitators across intervention characteristics, settings, individuals, and process, enabling cross-initiative comparisons and consistent language for policy and practice <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR organizes and presents barriers and facilitators to advance adoption across organizations</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR’s domains reveal common barriers and facilitators across diverse programs</cite>.
- Cyberbullying response: A structured taxonomy (psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, prevention/intervention) and conceptual map show how to design reporting tools, awareness campaigns, policy reforms, and UX interventions in unison <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Six-category barrier taxonomy with conceptual mapping guides prevention and response strategies</cite>.

Key distinctions to sharpen your conceptual map
- Barrier vs. facilitator: Barriers impede “use”; facilitators enable it; frameworks like CFIR operationalize both to design for win–win conversions (e.g., training and support convert effort expectancy barriers into ease-of-use facilitators) <cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR explicitly distinguishes constructs that positively or negatively influence implementation</cite>.
- Obstacle vs. opportunity: Negative barriers that obstruct also reveal design or policy opportunities; treat obstacles as diagnostic signals rather than merely targets for removal <cite id="317e1c0d-2">Resistance can highlight risks and misalignments, requiring root-cause understanding</cite>.
- Structural vs. proximal: Separate organizational/outer-setting constraints (networks, legitimacy) from individual/inner-setting perceptions (usefulness, ease) to avoid misattribution and to target the right levers <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Networks and legitimacy operate at the organizational level, while contingency adaptation aligns to context</cite><cite id="f40d5515-0">Perceived usefulness and ease function as proximal determinants of adoption</cite>.
- Static vs. dynamic: Avoid linear models when systems change rapidly; use adaptive-cycle and iterative feedback to sequence interventions and to manage evolving resistance and constraints <cite id="317e1c0d-1">The rapid pace of technological change requires continuous, adaptive management and feedback loops</cite>.

The UTAUT integrates elements from various technology acceptance theories, aiming to offer a unified framework for understanding the factors influencing individuals' acceptance and use of technology in organisational settings (Venkatesh et al., 2003). Snippet: In this sense, implementation may be a determinant of organizational survival; to the extent that implementing an innovation does not promote survival, implementation is unlikely to occur. Additionally, examining the barriers to implementation offers an opportunity to investigate overlap across theories and to advance theories that specify and explain cross-level influences (e.g., influences that span across organizational environment, organizational behavior, and provider behavior). 

Our paper also suggests that key organizational theories should be incorporated into implementation frameworks. Developers of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) did not draw upon the kinds of classic organizational theories that we advocate for implementation research, but the CFIR includes constructs that relate to some key organizational theory constructs [12]. For example, the CFIR's cosmopolitanism domain (i.e., the extent to which an organization is networked with others) suggests the importance of interagency relationships. RDT provides a rationale for including this construct: Organizations with stronger networks may facilitate implementation by increasing access to resources including information, influence, and funding [62]. Drawing on organizational theory, we can further specify and expand upon constructs included in implementation frameworks. 

Finally, the application of organizational theories to implementation has practical implications. Organizational theories suggest that managers should be aware of influences from the external environment that may influence adoption, implementation, and sustainment. TCE, for example, suggests that having established relationships with external organizations that influence implementation may promote implementation success. Institutional theory suggests that gaining legitimacy-regardless of whether it improves performance-may drive adoption decisions. In some cases, the drive to gain legitimacy may undermine the objectives of an implementation effort; organizational leaders may superficially implement an EBI, without effecting change, to conform to institutional pressures. Contingency theories suggest that successful implementation will likely require adaptation of an intervention to the manager's unique organizational context. RDT suggests that threats to maintaining autonomy or resources represent threats to implementation and sustainment. Organizational theory also encourages a skepticism of practice trends. In response to practice trends, researchers often assess strategies for accommodating these trends. In contrast, organization theory can help to alert practitioners and researchers to potential negative consequences of practice trends. For example, institutional theory suggests that following practice trends may confer legitimacy but not necessarily performance improvement.

Snippet: The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) guided the research. CFIR is a comprehensive framework that synthesizes core constructs from 29 prominent organizational and implementation science theories, with uniform language to promote generalizability across disciplines [23]. We chose CFIR because it is not specific to any intervention type (e.g., increasing protocol use) and allowed us to investigate common implementation barriers and facilitators across diverse interventions. Below is a comprehensive, theory-grounded review of “barriers,” “challenges,” and “obstacles,” their conceptual differences, and the theoretical foundations you can deploy for a master’s thesis. The review synthesizes cross-domain definitions, major models and frameworks, and practical ways to map and analyze barriers to use, with attention to how to build theoretical sensitivity and an actionable conceptual map.

Conceptual foundations: what are barriers, challenges, and obstacles?
Across domains, barriers, challenges, and obstacles are closely related yet carry distinct emphases. A baseline definition treats a barrier as anything that impedes progress toward a goal, with challenges and obstacles often used interchangeably to denote impediments that require removal, adaptation, or creative problem-solving to overcome <cite id="565a2ab8-0">Barriers are obstacles or challenges that hinder the progress or achievement of goals</cite><cite id="565a2ab8-1">Barriers are often impediments and obstacles that obstruct progress and the achievement of goals, and overcoming them requires creative management and mindset change</cite>. Conceptual metaphor work shows how “business is a journey,” where barriers are structured impediments such as entry barriers, switching barriers, and barriers to imitation—illustrating how domain-specific “barriers” become strategic constructs <cite id="565a2ab8-2">In business, barriers like entry barriers, barriers to imitation, and exit barriers illustrate numerous obstacles in business activities</cite>. Education provides a clear typology: internal (cognitive, emotional) versus external (ecological, institutional) learning barriers, together with teacher-facing challenges in addressing them, highlighting the duality of personal and contextual constraints <cite id="565a2ab8-3">Learning barriers impede knowledge/skill acquisition and can be internal (cognitive/emotional) or external (ecological/resources), with teachers facing challenges in identification, resource limitations, and classroom management</cite>. Cyberbullying research operationalizes barriers into six categories (psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, prevention/intervention) and visualizes them as a conceptual map—useful for structuring a comprehensive obstacle taxonomy and mitigation plan <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Barriers and challenges were categorized into psychological, social/cultural, awareness and reporting, legal and policy, technological, and prevention/intervention, and illustrated in a conceptual map</cite>.

Theoretical families organizing “barriers” to use and change

1) Individual behavior and technology acceptance (TAM/UTAUT/IRT)
Technology acceptance models treat barriers as determinant factors shaping intention and use. TAM posits perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as primary drivers; ease of use positively influences usefulness, and both shape adoption behavior <cite id="f40d5515-0">Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are the main determinants of technology acceptance, with ease of use positively influencing usefulness</cite>. UTAUT integrates determinants across eight prior theories into performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, and has demonstrated stronger explanatory power for usage intention and behavior than earlier models (often up to ~70% variance explained), making it a robust lens to identify barriers at individual and organizational levels <cite id="f40d5515-1">UTAUT integrates determinants from TRA, TAM, TPB, MM, MPCU, IDT, and SCT into performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions</cite><cite id="f40d5515-3">UTAUT identifies performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, and has shown higher explanatory power than prior models (up to ~70% of variance in intention and 50% in use)</cite><cite id="f40d5515-4">Compared with earlier models (17%–42% variance), UTAUT achieves up to 70% explanatory power, making it effective for analyzing technology acceptance</cite>. Innovation resistance theory (IRT) explicitly categorizes barriers into functional (risk, value, usage) and psychological (traditional, image) types, especially salient in early adoption stages and often integrated with UTAUT/TAM to diagnose adoption barriers <cite id="f40d5515-0">Innovation resistance theory categorizes innovation resistance into functional barriers (risk, value, usage) and psychological barriers (traditional, image), and is frequently integrated with UTAUT or TAM</cite>. These models offer measurable constructs (e.g., effort expectancy as a barrier, facilitating conditions as enablers), enabling empirical testing and intervention design in a master’s thesis.

2) Organizational change and resistance (Kotter, Lewin; multidimensional resistance)
Organizational transformation repeatedly encounters resistance as a key obstacle; change models emphasize that resistance must be managed, not merely eliminated, with strategies such as creating urgency, strong leadership, phased communication, and adaptive, iterative management <cite id="317e1c0d-0">Resistance to change is a common obstacle in organizational transformation and must be managed</cite><cite id="317e1c0d-1">Resistance emerges from individual fears (job loss, skill gaps) and structural issues (leadership, cultural misfit), with barriers including poor communication, low perceived value, and limited training; strategies include leadership commitment, phased communication, and adaptive piloting with feedback loops</cite>. Contemporary frameworks show resistance is multidimensional—cognitive, affective, and intentional—and may be outspoken or silent, deliberate or non-deliberate, directed at the process, change itself, or the technology; they also attend to who resists and over time, making resistance a signal guiding more resilient practices <cite id="317e1c0d-2">Resistance is multidimensional (cognitive, affective, intentional) and may be outspoken/silent, deliberate/non-deliberate, with temporal and stakeholder specificity; frameworks help understand and manage resistance as a signal for resilient practices</cite>. Adaptive-cycle and holistic approaches map where resistance concentrates across stages and how management styles and stakeholder needs interact with technological change, reinforcing that barriers are dynamic and context-contingent <cite id="317e1c0d-4">A holistic approach integrates the Adaptive Cycle of Resilience, Maslow’s theory, and organizational models to identify where resistance concentrates across stages and how management styles and stakeholder needs shape technological change</cite><cite id="f40d5515-1">Change models such as Lewin and Kotter underpin strategies to address resistance in technology adoption</cite>. Conceptually, TAM/UTAUT capture proximal, individual-level barriers, while organizational change theories capture distal, structural, cultural, and power-related barriers; together they cover the full barrier stack for “use.”

3) Socio-technical, institutional, and contingency perspectives (organizational theory, legitimacy, networks)
Implementation science shows barriers and facilitators span levels: intervention characteristics, inner/outer settings, individuals, and process. CFIR synthesizes 29 theories into five domains and 39 constructs, offering uniform language to compare barriers and facilitators across contexts and interventions, including networks/legitimacy and readiness—directly linking organizational theory to implementation barriers <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR constructs synthesize 29 organizational and implementation theories to identify, organize, and communicate barriers and facilitators across organizations</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Organizational theory specifies cross-level influences (environment to behavior), supports constructs like interagency networks (cosmopolitanism) for resource access, highlights legitimacy and contingency pressures, and cautions that superficial implementation can occur to gain legitimacy</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR’s five domains—intervention characteristics, inner setting, outer setting, individual characteristics, and process—provide a common structure for implementation barriers and facilitators across diverse initiatives</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-3">CFIR specifies 39 constructs across five domains influencing implementation, integrating determinant theories</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR provides a determinant framework with 26 constructs across five domains, is suited for studying barriers and facilitators, and is widely used for cross-setting comparisons</cite>. These frameworks align with socio-technical thinking: technical constraints (e.g., complexity, cost) interact with social-ecological constraints (e.g., culture, networks, legitimacy), and contingency theories argue that successful “use” requires adaptation to context; resistance may persist when interventions are not adapted to local norms and resources <cite id="8b19d7a4-1">Contingency theories suggest successful implementation requires adaptation to unique organizational context, while threats to autonomy or resources undermine sustainment; institutional pressures can drive superficial implementation for legitimacy</cite>. Conceptually, this positions barriers as emergent intersections of technical and socio-institutional layers, where “barriers to use” include misfit with existing practices, legitimacy deficits, and network-access constraints.

4) Complexity, chaos, and dynamic systems (adaptive cycles; iterative feedback)
Adaptive-cycle models (e.g., Panarchy/ACoR) depict organizations as complex systems where resistance and change interlock across stages (e.g., exploitation, conservation, release, reorganization), implying that barriers shift with system state and require staged, iterative responses. Integrating such models with motivation and management theories clarifies when resistance is most likely and how leadership and information systems can recalibrate pathways <cite id="317e1c0d-4">Resistance peaks at identifiable stages in the Adaptive Cycle; management styles and stakeholder needs shape outcomes, and information systems influence change trajectories</cite>. This emphasizes barriers as dynamic constraints within complex systems, not static impediments, motivating mixed-methods designs that capture feedback and evolution.

User-centered perspectives treat “barriers to use” as anti-affordances and pain points in interaction—frictions that hinder goals and must be removed or reframed through empathic design. Cyberbullying SLR exemplifies structured categorization of barriers across psychological, social/cultural, awareness/reporting, legal/policy, technological, and prevention/intervention domains; you can adapt this into “obstacle taxonomies” for your context, mapping each obstacle to user stories, personas, and journey stages and visualizing them in a system map <cite id="565a2ab8-4">Barriers and challenges were categorized into psychological, social/cultural, awareness and reporting, legal and policy, technological, and prevention/intervention, and illustrated in a conceptual map</cite>. Conceptually, barriers here are visible UX constraints plus latent, context-dependent constraints (e.g., policy or cultural norms), and challenges become hypotheses about redesigns to restore affordance–constraint balance.

For interventions and programs, CFIR offers the most widely used determinant framework to systematically elicit barriers and facilitators across five domains and 39 constructs, enabling cross-setting comparisons and consistent coding. It is not a single theory but a meta-framework that integrates organizational, sociocultural, and process determinants, and is increasingly used to compare barriers across multiple, distinct initiatives within one organization—a powerful approach for mapping organizational obstacles to adoption, implementation, and sustainment <cite id="8b19d7a4-0">CFIR provides a standard, evidence-based path to identify, organize, and communicate barriers and facilitators</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-2">CFIR’s five domains structure the analysis of common implementation barriers and facilitators across diverse initiatives</cite><cite id="8b19d7a4-4">CFIR’s scope, clarity, and widespread use enable comparison of barriers and facilitators within and across contexts</cite>. In practice, CFIR supports grounded coding of qualitative data (e.g., interviews, observations) and quantitative indicators (e.g., relative advantage, complexity, cost) into barrier/facilitator categories, which is ideal for a master’s thesis that integrates mixed methods.

- Barriers: structural or contextual impediments that limit the possibility of intended actions; can be positive (protective) or negative (impediments), and may be designed or emergent; negative barriers obstruct progress and require removal or work-around <cite id="565a2ab8-1">Barriers can be positively designed as protective mechanisms or negatively function as impediments/obstacles that obstruct progress and must be removed; overcoming them often requires creative thinking and mindset change</cite>.

Snippet: This linear model is often challenged by the rapid pace of technological development, which requires continuous adaptation rather than static stages. Kotter's (1995) eight steps to organizational change emphasize creating a sense of urgency and a reason for change, which helps employees understand and engage with the change process. Lapointe & Rivard (2005) view resistance to IT as a potential power-shifting medium within organizations. The use of technology can alter power dynamics among social groups and between organizations. This shift can be generational or educational, with younger or more educated employees better utilizing technology. Resistance, therefore, becomes an obstacle to be removed for successful IT system implementation. Bagayogo et al. (2013) argue against treating resistance at face value, advocating for understanding the root concerns, which may include quality issues or risks associated with new systems. Resistance can sometimes have a positive impact by highlighting potential flaws or risks. Shimoni (2017) identified three schools of thought on resistance to change: the individual psychological disposition perspective, the social context perspective, and the social construction perspective. He also proposed a fourth perspective, the habitus-oriented approach based on Bourdieu's action theory, which views resistance as an internalized and institutionalized part of an organization's social field. Smollan (2011) highlight the multidimensional nature of resistance, which includes cognitive, affective, and intentional components. Resistance can be expressed consciously or unconsciously, adding complexity to its understanding. Researchers and practitioners must address both observable and less detectable aspects of resistance, including emotional and affective responses. 

Resent work by (Fleron et al., 2023) presents a framework for encountering resistance, addressing both outspoken and silent, observable and non-observable, deliberate and nondeliberate actions of individuals and groups. The framework considers who is resisting, what is being resisted (the process, change itself, or technology), and the specific stakeholders involved. It also incorporates a temporal aspect, focusing on past, present, and future resistance. This framework aims to better understand and manage resistance to change in information systems-related projects, ultimately leading to more successful change initiatives.

Title: Navigating Resistance to Technological Change in Organizations: A Holistic Approach
Snippet: Organizational change driven by technological advancements presents both opportunities and challenges for modern enterprises. A key obstacle is a resistance to adopting new technologies, which can manifest through scepticism, fear of job displacement, perceived loss of control, and concerns about competence. This resistance poses significant barriers to the successful implementation and integration of technological innovations, leading to delays, inefficiencies, and missed opportunities for organisational growth and competitiveness. This research proposes a holistic approach to address the complex challenge of resistance to technological change. Drawing on theoretical frameworks such as the Adaptive Cycle of Resilience (ACoR) model, Maslow's Motivation Theory, and Keidel's organisational model, as well as practical strategies, the study examines the interplay between individuals, different management, organisational and societal needs in the context of technological transformation. The research explores the dynamic and uncertain nature of technological change, identifying the specific stages within the ACoR model where resistance is most likely to occur and the implications for effective management. It also investigates the role of various management styles in addressing resistance and uncovering the skills and knowledge individuals and teams require to navigate this challenge successfully. Furthermore, the paper delves into the diverse stakeholders involved in the technological change process, analysing their needs and concerns and offering strategies to balance these competing interests. The importance of information systems in facilitating organizational change and their influence on the change process and outcomes is also examined. By synthesising these insights, the study presents a comprehensive framework for organisations to foster innovation, inclusivity, and social responsibility in the face of resistance to technological change. The findings offer valuable guidance for practitioners and scholars seeking to enable successful technological transformations and promote positive outcomes for all stakeholders.

Kotter's (1995) eight steps to organizational change emphasize creating a sense of urgency and a reason for change, which helps employees understand and engage with the change process. Lapointe & Rivard (2005) view resistance to IT as a potential power-shifting medium within organizations. The use of technology can alter power dynamics among social groups and between organizations. This shift can be generational or educational, with younger or more educated employees better utilizing technology. Resistance, therefore, becomes an obstacle to be removed for successful IT system implementation. Bagayogo et al. (2013) argue against treating resistance at face value, advocating for understanding the root concerns, which may include quality issues or risks associated with new systems. Resistance can sometimes have a positive impact by highlighting potential flaws or risks. Shimoni (2017) identified three schools of thought on resistance to change: the individual psychological disposition perspective, the social context perspective, and the social construction perspective. He also proposed a fourth perspective, the habitus-oriented approach based on Bourdieu's action theory, which views resistance as an internalized and institutionalized part of an organization's social field. Smollan (2011) highlight the multidimensional nature of resistance, which includes cognitive, affective, and intentional components. Resistance can be expressed consciously or unconsciously, adding complexity to its understanding. Researchers and practitioners must address both observable and less detectable aspects of resistance, including emotional and affective responses. 

Resent work by (Fleron et al., 2023) presents a framework for encountering resistance, addressing both outspoken and silent, observable and non-observable, deliberate and nondeliberate actions of individuals and groups. The framework considers who is resisting, what is being resisted (the process, change itself, or technology), and the specific stakeholders involved. It also incorporates a temporal aspect, focusing on past, present, and future resistance. This framework aims to better understand and manage resistance to change in information systems-related projects, ultimately leading to more successful change initiatives.

snippet.text: Organizational change driven by technological advancements presents both opportunities and challenges for modern enterprises. A key obstacle is a resistance to adopting new technologies, which can manifest through scepticism, fear of job displacement, perceived loss of control, and concerns about competence. This resistance poses significant barriers to the successful implementation and integration of technological innovations, leading to delays, inefficiencies, and missed opportunities for organisational growth and competitiveness. This research proposes a holistic approach to address the complex challenge of resistance to technological change. Drawing on theoretical frameworks such as the Adaptive Cycle of Resilience (ACoR) model, Maslow's Motivation Theory, and Keidel's organisational model, as well as practical strategies, the study examines the interplay between individuals, different management, organisational and societal needs in the context of technological transformation. The research explores the dynamic and uncertain nature of technological change, identifying the specific stages within the ACoR model where resistance is most likely to occur and the implications for effective management. It also investigates the role of various management styles in addressing resistance and uncovering the skills and knowledge individuals and teams require to navigate this challenge successfully. Furthermore, the paper delves into the diverse stakeholders involved in the technological change process, analysing their needs and concerns and offering strategies to balance these competing interests. The importance of information systems in facilitating organizational change and their influence on the change process and outcomes is also examined. By synthesising these insights, the study presents a comprehensive framework for organisations to foster innovation, inclusivity, and social responsibility in the face of resistance to technological change. The findings offer valuable guidance for practitioners and scholars seeking to enable successful technological transformations and promote positive outcomes for all stakeholders.

Title: Organizational theory for dissemination and implementation research
Snippet: In this sense, implementation may be a determinant of organizational survival; to the extent that implementing an innovation does not promote survival, implementation is unlikely to occur. Additionally, examining the barriers to implementation offers an opportunity to investigate overlap across theories and to advance theories that specify and explain cross-level influences (e.g., influences that span across organizational environment, organizational behavior, and provider behavior). 

Our paper also suggests that key organizational theories should be incorporated into implementation frameworks. Developers of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) did not draw upon the kinds of classic organizational theories that we advocate for implementation research, but the CFIR includes constructs that relate to some key organizational theory constructs [12]. For example, the CFIR's cosmopolitanism domain (i.e., the extent to which an organization is networked with others) suggests the importance of interagency relationships. RDT provides a rationale for including this construct: Organizations with stronger networks may facilitate implementation by increasing access to resources including information, influence, and funding [62]. Drawing on organizational theory, we can further specify and expand upon constructs included in implementation frameworks. 

Finally, the application of organizational theories to implementation has practical implications. Organizational theories suggest that managers should be aware of influences from the external environment that may influence adoption, implementation, and sustainment. TCE, for example, suggests that having established relationships with external organizations that influence implementation may promote implementation success. Institutional theory suggests that gaining legitimacy-regardless of whether it improves performance-may drive adoption decisions. In some cases, the drive to gain legitimacy may undermine the objectives of an implementation effort; organizational leaders may superficially implement an EBI, without effecting change, to conform to institutional pressures. Contingency theories suggest that successful implementation will likely require adaptation of an intervention to the manager's unique organizational context. RDT suggests that threats to maintaining autonomy or resources represent threats to implementation and sustainment. Organizational theory also encourages a skepticism of practice trends. In response to practice trends, researchers often assess strategies for accommodating these trends. In contrast, organization theory can help to alert practitioners and researchers to potential negative consequences of practice trends. For example, institutional theory suggests that following practice trends may confer legitimacy but not necessarily performance improvement.

Title: Barriers and facilitators to implementing priority inpatient initiatives in the safety net setting
Snippet: The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) guided the research. CFIR is a comprehensive framework that synthesizes core constructs from 29 prominent organizational and implementation science theories, with uniform language to promote generalizability across disciplines [23]. CFIR describes five domains theorized to influence implementation success: [1] intervention characteristics, [2] inner setting, [3] outer setting, [4] characteristics of the individuals involved, and [5] the process of implementation. We chose CFIR because it is not specific to any intervention type (e.g., increasing protocol use) and allowed us to investigate common implementation barriers and facilitators across diverse interventions. Our application of CFIR is novel. Although CFIR has been widely used in implementation science research to describe how individual interventions are promoted and adopted [24], this is one of the first studies to use CFIR as a tool for collectively analyzing the implementation experiences, barriers, and facilitators of multiple, programmatically distinct initiatives. Applying CFIR in this way leverages the framework's ability to synthesize core factors influencing implementation processes and reveal meaningful themes across diverse initiatives whose only initial commonality was that implementation occurred in a SNH.

Snippet: This review used the CFIR framework to analyze the implementation barriers and facilitators documented in the reviewed studies. Title: Barriers and facilitators to implementation of nutrition-related actions in school settings in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs): a qualitative systematic review using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR)
Snippet: The CFIR is a determinant framework well suited for the study of barriers and facilitators to implementation [18]. The framework was built on existing theories, and although it is one-dimensional without specifying the relationships between constructs and distinguishing between different ecological levels [18], it captures and clearly defines a comprehensive list of barriers and facilitators [18,19]. The CFIR is also the most widely used determinant framework in implementation science, which enables the comparison of findings within and across disciplines and in different contexts and settings [20]. Its scope, clarity of constructs, wide usage, and our previous experience with the framework were the main reasons for choosing it for this review. The CFIR was used for the coding and analysis of the data extracted from the included articles.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The verification criterion is 'Any non-empty answer is acceptable.' The answer is substantial, comprehensive, and far exceeds the minimum requirement of being non-empty. It provides an extensive literature review with multiple sections, theoretical frameworks, conceptual distinctions, and practical guidance for a master's thesis.
other_issues: The answer is extremely lengthy and may overwhelm a master's student. While comprehensive, it could benefit from more concise structuring or a clearer hierarchy of essential vs. supplementary content.

Some citations appear stretched beyond their original scope. For example, reference [1] is from a study on 'Enhancing Motivation through Leisure Activities in Schizophrenia' but is cited for a general definition of barriers. While the definition may be accurate, the domain-specificity of sources is not always acknowledged.

Reference [2] is cited extensively for conceptual distinctions between barriers as 'positive' vs 'negative,' but this appears to be from a logistics study about self-employed saleswomen in Manaus. The generalizability of these conceptual distinctions to other domains is assumed rather than demonstrated.

The integration of multiple frameworks (TAM/UTAUT, CFIR, organizational change theories, etc.) is thorough but may create conceptual overload. The answer would benefit from clearer guidance on when to use which framework based on research context.

Some theoretical connections are asserted rather than demonstrated. For instance, the claim that 'TAM/UTAUT capture proximal, individual-level barriers, while organizational change theories capture distal, structural, cultural, and power-related barriers' is conceptually reasonable but presented as fact without explicit support from the references.

The 'conceptual map' and 'barrier taxonomy' are described extensively but not actually visualized, which may limit practical utility for a visual learner or someone trying to operationalize the framework.
Minor redundancy: several key points (e.g., CFIR's five domains, UTAUT's determinants) are repeated multiple times throughout the document, which could be streamlined.
judgment.summary: The answer comprehensively satisfies the verification criterion by providing an extensive, theory-grounded literature review of barriers, challenges, and obstacles. It synthesizes multiple theoretical frameworks, distinguishes between concepts, and offers practical guidance for a master's thesis. However, the answer suffers from excessive length, some citations from highly domain-specific sources being applied broadly without qualification, and occasional conceptual assertions that exceed what the references strictly support. Despite these issues, the core content is substantive and useful.

Researchers often begin with conceptual distinctions among “barriers,” “challenges,” and “obstacles,” but in practice they are frequently used interchangeably and operationalized through diverse methodological lenses (qualitative coding schemes, checklists, and survey items), leading to both systematic categorizations and ad hoc, context-dependent measures. - Definitions and synonymy: Conceptual definitions typically treat barriers as circumstances or obstacles that impede progress; “challenge” and “obstacle” are used as equivalents in many applied texts and reviews. <cite id="448072c0-1">Barriers are described as obstacles or challenges that hinder goal progress</cite> <cite id="448072c0-4">and dictionaries/lexicography treat “barrier,” “challenge,” and “issue/problem” as interchangeable alternatives in applied contexts</cite>.

- Graduate theses and programs: Reviews of graduate students’ methodological journeys report specific challenges (e.g., distinguishing qualitative design from data, writing thesis, presenting work) and obstacles (e.g., insufficient supervision, resource gaps), often operationalized through structured instruments and qualitative narratives. <cite id="8e890fab-0">Postgraduate students encounter obstacles in formulating research methodologies and thesis write-ups; faculty involvement and academic culture differences compound difficulties</cite> <cite id="8e890fab-1">and cross-sectional surveying isolates structural and institutional barriers with quantitative evidence of their impact on research self-efficacy</cite> <cite id="8e890fab-2">phenomenological analysis of graduate success surfaces institutional barriers (time constraints, gender roles) and enablers (supervision, flexibility), coding distinct challenge types</cite>.

Comparative patterns across domains and methods
- Convergence: Across education and health, “barriers” are most often operationalized through either explicit taxonomies (individual/organizational/operational) or through iterative qualitative coding that extracts distinct domains; “challenges” and “obstacles” are commonly collapsed into barrier-type measures but retain distinct colloquial meanings tied to internal vs external, structural vs cultural, and capability vs motivational strata. <cite id="448072c0-3">Structured barrier categories provide a shared language for comparing and guiding interventions</cite> <cite id="a445babc-2">while grounded theory’s axial/selective coding consolidates rich, distinct challenge domains from interviews</cite> <cite id="448072c0-4">and reviews often aggregate barriers/challenges/obstacles under a unified construct without standardized alignment</cite>.

- Terminology matters for methods: If a thesis distinguishes barriers vs challenges vs obstacles conceptually, it should choose methods and instruments aligned to each category (e.g., capability-focused barriers via capability assessments; cultural/relational challenges via semistructured interviews and axial coding; motivational obstacles via validated motivation/confidence scales). <cite id="448072c0-3">Categorical frameworks (individual/organizational/operational) can structure measurement and comparability</cite> <cite id="a445babc-2">and grounded theory procedures provide systematic routes to differentiate nuanced challenge domains</cite> <cite id="8e890fab-1">whereas quantitative barriers can be indexed via structured questionnaires and linked to outcomes through regression/χ2</cite>.

Researchers who theoretically distinguish barriers, challenges, and obstacles tend to operationalize them differently depending on method and context: barriers are frequently categorized (individual/organizational/operational) or measured via structured items and indices; challenges often surface through qualitative coding and mixed-method designs capturing processual and motivational domains; obstacles are commonly operationalized as concrete impediments (skills deficits, policies, resource gaps) quantified with questionnaires and linked to outcomes, though many studies collapse these terms. Title: Using Program Theory to Evaluate a Graduate College Student Development Program
Snippet: Background: The “3 Minute Presentation” is a graduate student competition based off the more popular “3 Minute Thesis” competition. The program aims to help graduate students learn to inform others of their research in a quick and accessible manner. Programs to engage graduate students more deeply in their education require evaluation to determine if they are useful and effective at meeting their intended goals. Evaluation literature in graduate educational programs is currently limited, but increasingly needed for both the field and the students served. 
  
Purpose: Development and testing of a program-theory evaluation to understand participation, recruitment, preparation, training, skills, and confidence of graduate students engaging in a “3 Minute Presentation” competition at a state university. 
  
Setting: Institution of Higher Education 
  
  
 
 
Intervention: 3 Minute Presentation competition 
  
Research Design:  Mixed-method program-theory evaluation

Title: Disrupting the Narrative on Recruiting Graduate Students of Color in Counselor Education
Snippet: The constant comparative method of data analysis, a signature element of grounded theory (Birks & Mills, 2011), was utilized in this study. The constant comparative method traditionally involves three phases of data analysis (open, axial, and selective), is systematic and structured, and provides a trail of evidence to support conclusions (Charmaz, 2014;Jones et al., 2014). We began data analysis upon completion of the eighth interview; this allowed us to test tentative hypotheses on the remaining participants -a practice known as theoretical sampling (Corbin & Strauss, 2015). As is consistent with a CRT framework, we focused on issues of race through data analysis. 

The first phase of data analysis in the constant comparative method is open coding (Charmaz, 2014). During this phase we conducted independent line-by-line readings of each interview transcript, with the goal of developing a nuanced understanding of the data (Charmaz, 2014). We then met as a group to develop consensus on codes. At the end of open coding, 218 coded segments of data were identified that ranged in length from a couple of lines to a paragraph. To respect participants' voices, we attempted to use their words as names for codes. A total of 57 unique codes were identified during open coding, including advocacy, campus diversity, professional role model, and program flexibility. 

The second phase of coding, axial coding, took place once all participant interviews were completed and open coding had concluded. During this phase, codes were first compared within each participant and then across all participants. The goal was to consolidate similar codes and eliminate codes that did not relate to the phenomenon under investigation. At the end of this process 14 codes remained, including: admissions process; diversity; role models and mentors; and work, school, life balance. 

During selective coding, the final phase of data analysis, the goal was to develop a theory that described the motivation of students of color for pursuing counselor education. Similar codes were again consolidated and others were organized thematically into factors. Upon completion of this process, three factors were identified that described the motivation and support that inspired graduate students of color to pursue counselor education.

Title: Courage, Honesty, and Evaluation in the Apprehensive University
Snippet: A consistent question in education is how to evaluate the degree to which universities and their programs are meeting the claims they make on their webpages and other materials, which entice students and faculty alike to join their collegiate community. Misalignments between what is promised and what is provided harm all community members but have disproportionate effects on students of color. It is therefore an ethical imperative for the higher education sector to undertake system wide evaluations because of the ever-rising financial and emotional costs of graduate education. For educators and administrators alike, this means systematically interrogating data to identify unseen patterns, challenge assumptions, and ask both critical and highly uncomfortable questions; for educators, this may include a truthful assessment of our own practices and assumptions. We propose drawing from the field of program evaluation and using theory-driven evaluation as a specific framework to understand graduate education process and outcomes. This conceptual paper links together existing literatures and is augmented by the authors’ reflection and dialogue about their experiences designing and implementing graduate education across several institutions. We end with a call for courage and honesty in carefully evaluating graduate education for the betterment of all students, faculty, and administrators.
